happens to an object that has an unbalanced force acting on it.

Noise and Health

‘We don’t always realise that noise can be a danger to our health. A ‘noise’
is often defined as ‘a loud, disagreeable sound’. Yet the same sound can
be either pleasant or a nuisance — it depends on the person hearing it.

What you think is ‘music’ might be ‘noise’ to older people. HIGH
NOISE
Noise is a problem to people who live in busy cities — they are continually AREA

exposed to loud noises, This noise can be from ordinary traffic, airports,
trains and trams, building work and machinery. Such types of noise can
make life uncomfortable for people living near these sources of noise.
Exposure to loud noise, for example, loud discos and concerts, can damage hearing or even cause deafness.
People who have had prolonged exposure to loud noise may suffer from headaches, tiredness and stress.

Noises are measured in units called decibels (dB). Special sound meters are used to measure loudness.
Zero decibels is the threshold of audibility, that is, the weakest sound the human ear can hear. Sounds
above 140 decibels (‘the threshold of pain’) hurt your ears and can cause permanent damage. If you
whisper, this will give a sound level of about 20 decibels, talking normally will give about 60 decibels,
whereas loud rock music registers at about 120 decibels.

We try to keep unwelcome sounds to a minimum. Traffic noise can be a problem so, in the exhaust systems
of cars, mufflers (silencers) are included to quieten the noise made by the engine. Insulation can also be
used in machinery to reduce its noise level. People working with noisy machines wear ear protectors or
earmuffs to reduce the amount of noise entering their ears.

Radiation

Radiation: any form of energy radiated (sent out) from a source,

Many people, when they hear the word ‘radiation’, think of nuclear reactions and radioactivity, but the
word means much more than that. Three main classes of radiation include electromagnetic radiation
(EMR), nuclear radiation, and cosmic radiation. All three types of radiation can travel in a vacuum,

Infra red (IR), ultra-violet (UV), visible (white) light and radio waves are examples of electromagnetic
radiation, Radioactivity is a type of nuclear radiation and cosmic radiation (or cosmic rays) come from
the sun and other objects in outer space. The sun releases cosmic rays during spectacular eruptions
called solar flares,

If you have ever lain on a beach and got a suntan, then the change in skin colour was caused by UV rays
from the sun. If you switch on an electric iron, after a while, without touching it, you can feel heat being
given off. Heat is a form of IR, which we cannot see. Radio signals are not just transmitted on Earth but occur
naturally from outer space, for example from stars, and can be detected on Earth by large radio telescopes.

EMR is always around us and is a form of energy associated
with electric and magnetic fields. It behaves like a wave and
travels through space at the speed of light, 300 000 kilometres
per second. There are different types of electromagnetic
radiation. Each type has a different wavelength and frequency,
but the same speed, Wavelength is measured in metres. The
frequency of a wave is the number of cycles per second
passing a certain point. The unit of frequency is Hertz or Hz.
One cycle per second is 1 Hz. Different wavelengths of EMR
carry different amounts of energy. Short-wavelength radiation
carries more energy than long-wavelength radiation.

Large, unstable atoms (radioisotopes) can break up and give off energy (gamma rays and X-rays) and
particles, Gamma rays and X-rays pass through solid objects and can be used to take pictures

Erosion: the removal or transportation of rock fragments.

The Atmosphere and
the Greenhouse Effect

Greenhouses are used to grow plants that would not thrive in outdoor conditions. In a greenhouse, the
walls are made of a transparent material, such as glass. The glass allows solar radiation (sunlight) through.

Balance in Nature

Ecosystem: a space containing organisms interacting with each other and their surroundings.

If an ecosystem has existed successfully for a long time, then the populations (members of a particular
species) are usually stable. This occurs when all of the organisms in an ecosystem are reasonably
compatible with each other and their environment. If numbers do change, this often happens at regular
intervals in a way that can be forecast, for example, in line with changes of seasons.

An ecosystem can be upset by the arrival of a new species or the loss of an existing one.

1 Apart from living creatures, what factors can change an ecosystem?

Cattle were first brought to Australia by sailing ships late in the eighteenth century. Due to the long voyages
many organisms were either left behind or died on the way. These included both beneficial and
pathogenic creatures. The dung beetle was one example. Dung beetles lay eggs in cattle dung. When the
larvae hatch out they eat the dung, This makes sure that the compounds present in the dung are returned
to the soil. It also keeps down the number of flies (which also breed in the dung) and increases the area
available for pasture. There are dung beetles native to Australia, but these tend to eat native wildlife dung
and do not eat the dung of introduced cattle.

If cattle are introduced without dung beetles then they are likely to have an adverse (hostile) effect on their
new environment. Because flies tend to eat dung, their numbers will increase — with the obvious
consequences. Some environmental organisations monitor the number of dung beetles. Dung beetles are
killed by some cattle drenches (medicine). It has been suggested that different species of dung beetles
should be introduced from overseas.

Building Materials

Stone has been used for thousands of years to make buildings, bridges and works of art.
1 Give two reasons why stone is used as a construction material.

Types of stone used for building include sandstone, granite, limestone and marble. The physical
characteristics of the type of stone will determine how it is used for building. For example, sandstone is
soft and easily cut from quarries; granite is much stronger than sandstone, limestone, and marble, and
marble is very popular for making statues and monuments due to its colour and lustre.

2 What disadvantage might there be in granite being such a strong stone?
Granite is more resistant to weathering than most other types of stone.
3 What does ‘resistant to weathering’ mean?

Sandstone and limestone are sedimentary rocks, that is they are made up of fine grains that have been
compressed together over a period of time, Granite is an igneous rock which means it was once molten and
has cooled and solidified. Marble is a metamorphic rock, that is it has been changed by heat and pressure.

Limestone, chalk and marble are all forms of calcium carbonate (CaCO,). Limestone is used as a raw
material in the manufacture of lime (calcium oxide CaO) and cement. Concrete is made from cement, water
{H,O), sand (mainly silicon dioxide, SiO,) and small stones.

Concrete is a very common building material. It is strong (and can be made even stronger by adding steel
reinforcing), durable, fairly cheap and can be poured into many different shapes.

dried in the sun. Bricks can resist weathering, are versatile and

Components of
Ecosystems

The environment is the conditions in which a plant or animal lives. An environment consists of living
(biotic) and non-living (abiotic) components. Abiotic components include things like air temperature, soil
pH, and so on.

1 Name two other possible abiotic components in an environment.

Ecology is the study of living things and their environment. The place where a plant or animal lives is its
habitat. There are many types of habitat in Australia, such as ocean and rainforests.

2 Name and describe two other types of habitat in Australia.

Population means all the members of a particular species (related organisms) found in an area. An
ecosystem is a group of living things together with their habitat or environment. You rarely find a single
type of organism living on its own. Populations of different species can be found sharing a habitat. There
is usually interaction with other species. When there is a collection of different species that exist with
others, this is a community, Koalas, for example, breed and live in the trees.

3 What do eucalypts provide for koalas?

The trees, in turn, need water, sunshine and nutrients from the soil. The soil is made up of the remains of
plants and animals that have rotted down, There are three categories of populations: producers, consumers
and decomposers.

Green plants are producers. They are the first link in all food chains. They contain chlorophyll and so can
photosynthesise, This process produces a food called glucose (a type of sugar) and also oxygen. It uses the
energy of the sun to drive the reaction. This solar energy is converted to stored chemical energy in plants.

4 What would happen to life on Earth if all the green plants suddenly died?

Animals are consumers. If they eat plants, they are first-order consumers or herbivores. The chemical
energy in the green plants is transferred to the animal when it eats the plant.

The biosphere is the region of the Earth that can support life. This includes the surface of the Earth, the
deepest depths of water and out to about 10 km into the atmosphere. You may notice other ‘spheres’

the way water is in the water cycle. Others like coal and oil are non-renewable.

Energy Transfer

Energy can be described as ‘the ability to do work’. It can take several forms, such as sound, light,
movement and heat. The unit of energy is the joule, which has the symbol J. The joule is very small so
we tend to use kJ (kilojoules) or MJ (megajoules). There are a thousand joules in a kilojoule and a million
joules in a megajoule. The average adult will need in the region of 5 MJ of energy a day to maintain health.
A typical power drill or hair drier may be rated at 500 watts. This means that it uses 500 joules per second.

Consider a wood barbecue. When wood bums it is reacting
with the oxygen in the air. This is an example of combustion.
Carbon dioxide (CO, ) is one of the products of this reaction.
The reaction heats up the surroundings, so heat is given out.
This is an exothermic reaction. ‘Exo’ comes from the Greek and
means ‘out’. Heat energy is given out by the reacting system.

‘Trees take in energy from the sun. They grow by a chemical
change called photosynthesis, Carbon dioxide from the air
combines with water to make new substances. This is an
endothermic reaction. ‘Endo’ also comes from the Greek and
means ‘in’. Energy is taken in by the system.

Carbon dioxide + Water —> Glucose + Oxygen

Green plants are producers — they make their own food. They contain chlorophyll and thus can
photosynthesise. This process produces a food called glucose (a type of sugar) and also oxygen.

This process uses the energy of the sun (solar energy) to drive the reaction. This solar energy is converted
to stored chemical energy in plants. This energy is used for growth by the plant and to provide energy for
the plant during darkness when photosynthesis cannot take place.

Without organisms which photosynthesise (such as green plants) and organisms which live in water (such
as phytoplankton), there would be no animal life. Animals would have no food to eat and no oxygen to

Energy from Biomass

With fossil fuels running out, the world needs renewable energy sources — energy sources that can be
made again as fast as they are used up. Plant material is an example of biomass (biological mass) which
is a good renewable energy source. Biomass is material which is living or has been living.

Plants are able to trap the sun’s energy using the chlorophyll in their leaves. They use the energy to convert
carbon dioxide and water to carbohydrate and oxygen.

1 What is this process of energy conversion called?

Carbohydrates store energy. When they are burned in air, this energy is released. Wood has been a
traditional fuel for many cultures. It is renewable, and is easily stored and transported. It can be converted
to charcoal (carbon) by heating in the absence of air. Although burning wood releases carbon dioxide into
the air, this is absorbed by the next generation of trees. Trees take a long time to grow and forests take up
a considerable area of land which could otherwise be used for housing or farming.

Ethanol has the formula CH,CH,OH and is an alcohol (alkanol). In Brazil, many cars (approximately 20%)
run on ethanol rather than petrol, Sugar cane is a fast-growing tropical plant. The sugar (sucrose) it
provides can be fermented to make ethanol, The fermented mixture is distilled to give pure ethanol.
Ethanol is an excellent liquid fuel that can be used instead of petrol in cars (with slight modifications to
the engine) or can be mixed with petrol. When ethanol burns it produces carbon dioxide and water.
Ethanol itself is a clean, renewable fuel, but it needs a very large area to grow sugar cane, and the processes
of refining sugar and ethanol do cause pollution.

Many plants produce vegetable oils — sunflower oil and peanut oil are examples. These oils could be used
as fuels in the future. Scientists are trying to find ways of making diesel engines run efficiently using

vegetable oils.

Fuels

Fuels: substances that produce heat or power during combustion.

A fuel is a substance which gives out heat energy when it burns. Most fuels need to combine with oxygen
(©) in order to burn to release their energy. Another name for burning is combustion. When carbon-based
fuels burn they give out carbon dioxide (CO,) and water (H,0). Reactions giving out heat are called
exothermic reactions.

Many of the fuels we use are fossil fuels. They are the remains of organic (living) matter from millions of
years ago. They consist mainly of hydrocarbons — compounds containing the elements carbon (C) and
hydrogen (H) only. Coal, oil and natural gas (methane, CH,) are the major fossil fuels.

Coal is the remains of ferns, trees and other plants that lived about 300 million years ago, when most of
the Earth was covered in swamps or forests, These plants stored energy from the sun in making their food
via the process of photosynthesis, When trees died, they fell and gradually became covered by layers of
vegetation. As time went on, the layers were crushed into the Earth, often by earthquakes, volcanic
eruptions or layers of mud and sediment.

The dead trees were squashed by the layers above. This pressure and heat from inside the Earth changed
the trees which eventually turned into seams of coal. Much of this coal lies deep underground, covered by
layers of sediment. To mine these underground deposits of coal, deep shafts must be dug. Some coal seams
have been pushed to the surface by earth movements. This coal can be mined by open-cast mining, once
the surface rock has been bulldozed away.

Glass

Glass has been used for over 4000 years to make containers and ornaments. More recently it has been used
for windows. Glass is a poor electrical and thermal conductor. Glass is neither a ‘proper’ solid nor a liquid
but is a ‘super cooled liquid’. Over hundreds of years, glass can very slowly flow and change shape. The
most commonly used glass (used in windows, jars, drinking vessels and so on) is soda glass. The raw
materials used in the manufacture of this type of glass are sand (silica, silicon dioxide), sodium carbonate
(‘soda’) and calcium carbonate (limestone).

‘Crystal’ glass contains lead oxide, is heavy and refracts (bends) light well, It is used in making ‘costume’
jewellery, lenses and prisms. Glasses containing lead are used to protect people working with radioactivity.

Laboratory glassware is made of borosilicate glass (Pyrex™) and contains borax. This
is also used to make cooking containers. It is strong, heat and chemical resistant.

Vehicle windshields are made of laminated glass. This consists of two sheets of thin
plate glass with a layer of plastic in between. The glass used to make lenses in
spectacles, cameras, microscopes, and telescopes needs to be very pure and free of
distortion, Although heavier than plastic, and more likely to shatter when dropped,
glass does not scratch as easily as plastic.

Fibre optics is the branch of optics (the study of light) dealing with the transmission of light through fibres
or thin rods of glass. Light can travel through the fibre over long distances with very low loss, even if the
fibre is curved. Optical fibres are used in medical instruments for viewing inside the human body and for
laser surgery, One growing application of optical fibres is in communication, where cables can carry much
more information than the equivalent copper cable.

Iron and Steel

With the exception of certain meteorites, iron (Fe) does not occur native (uncombined with other
elements) in the Earth’s crust. There are many compounds of iron, such as iron sulfide (iron pyrites, FeS,),
haematite (Fe,0,) and magnetite (Fe,O,). Iron is the second most abundant metal in the Earth’s crust,
Because it can be relatively easily extracted from its ores and because it has useful physical properties, it
has become a metal of considerable importance.

Iron is produced in a blast furnace. This is a tapered, cylindrical tower approximately 30 to 40 metres high.
It is constructed of steel and is lined with special heat resistant (refractory) bricks.

A blast furnace works continuously and can produce more than 1000 tonnes of iron every 24 hours. The
taw materials are iron ore (for example, haematite), coke (carbon, C), limestone (calcium carbonate,
CaCO,) and air, Coke is obtained from coal.

The molten iron formed flows to the bottom of the blast furnace, Impurities (mainly calcium silicate) form
as slag, floating on top of the molten iron. Slag and iron are tapped off, and allowed to cool and solidify. The
iron produced is still relatively impure and is known as cast iron or pig iron. It contains about 4% carbon. It
is very hard but brittle. This type of iron is only used for objects which are not likely to be bent when used.

Pure iron is not a good material for building things. It corrodes (rusts) very easily and is soft. Most iron
produced in blast furnaces is turned into steel, an alloy (mixture) of iron. There are thousands of types of
steel and their properties will depend on the other elements added. The impurities present are removed
from molten cast iron in a special furnace and other elements are added in careful proportions. Mild steel
is commonly used for car bodies. It is cheap, easily shaped and relatively strong.

Ores and Metals

Ore: a mineral containing enough of a metal to make it worthwhile mining.

Ores consist of metals chemically combined with other elements — usually oxygen (forming an oxide) or
sulfur (making a sulfide). Some metals can be found native, that is, uncombined. Gold (Au), silver (Ag)
and copper (Cu) are examples of native metals. Jewellery, ornaments and coins have been made from silver
and gold for a very long time. Both are attractive metals, resist corrosion, are relatively scarce and are
therefore, valuable.

The amount of metal ores in the Earth's crust is limited, We cannot continue digging them up forever.
Sooner or later there will not be enough to be worth mining. The amount of metal ore we know is worth
getting out is called the reserve of that ore, The table below shows one estimate of approximately how long
metal ores will last if we continue to use them at the present rate,

not yet discovered, Recycling is one way of making metal supplies last longer. This means that metals are
melted down and used again. Over 90% of gold we use is recycled, though this only happens to 50% of iron
(Fe). We can do more to recycle metals now, and in the future we will need to do so. It has been estimated
that the average family of four will throw away about 25 kg of aluminium (Al) and 70 kg of iron per year.

Some metals are more abundant than others, The prices of metals depend on how plentiful they are, how

Human beings have kept records since at least the last Ice Age, about 20 000 years ago. Many systems of
characters and symbols have been used. The Sumerians (who lived in a region similar to modern day Iraq)
pressed wedge-shaped marks into wet clay about 5000 years ago, using a language known as cuneiform.
Other civilisations have used marks on parchment (goat or sheep skin) or vellum (calfskin), The ancient
Egyptians wrote on papyrus, a plant-based material. Paper was invented by the Chinese nearly 2000 years
ago. Paper can be produced from almost any plant material fibre containing cellulose. Wood pulp is the most
common (95% of total production) but bamboo, cotton (and similar fibres) and straw can also be used.

Here is a simplified sequence for making paper:

wood is made into small wood chips

chips are turned to pulp by being ground and/or by being treated with chemicals

the pulp is bleached

substances are added to the pulp to give paper colour, texture and lustre

water is added

the pulp is passed through rollers, where the water is removed by squeezing and heating
the finished paper is wound on reels.

‘To make paper, a large amount of raw materials is needed. It also requires a large amount of energy and
generates a large amount of effluent (waste). Many people are concerned with the chemicals (often based
on chlorine) used to bleach paper. Environmentally friendly brands of paper have been produced which
are either not bleached or are bleached using oxygen,

Recycling paper can help cut down on the amount of wood needed for paper.
However, recycled paper cannot be used by itself to make high quality paper.
It needs to be either used to make packaging materials, or to be mixed with
new wood pulp. Before printed paper can be recycled it has to be ‘de-inked’.
Australian industry recycles a large quantity of the paper it uses.

Pests cause major damage to crops all over the world. Pests include insects, plants, animals and even

Pollution

A substance pollutes when its presence in air, water or soil harms living things.

The main cause of air pollution is the burning of fossil fuels, such as coal and oil. This happens in factories,
power stations, houses and the engines of cars, buses, and aeroplanes. Poisonous gases from chimneys are
quickly spread out in the air but, if there is not too much of them, they can change into less harmful
substances over time.

The smoke produced by burning contains tiny particles of dust, which are mainly carbon (C). This dust
settles on plant leaves, cutting out some of the light taken in by the plants and so reducing photosynthesis,
People also breathe in the dust and this can worsen illnesses such as asthma and bronchitis.

Sulfur dioxide (SO,) is a gas produced by burning fossil fuels. It can dissolve in water vapour, forming an
acid, which falls as acid rain. As well as damaging buildings, plants and wildlife this can affect people's lungs.

Petrol and diesel (internal combustion)
engines, especially when they are not
running properly, produce fumes which
gather in city streets. As well as sulfur
dioxide, carbon monoxide (CO) and oxides
of nitrogen are produced. Some petrol
(‘super’) contains lead (Pb). Cars burning
leaded petrol emit lead compounds, These
can collect in the bodies of people living in
areas where traffic is dense. Lead
compounds can cause damage to health —
especially that of the brain so Lead
Replacement Petrol (LRP) is now being
used, Lead was once used for water pipes. It
is soft, easily worked and lasts for a long

Rocks and Minerals

All of the rocks in the Earth’s crust are composed of minerals. A mineral is a chemical compound which
occurs naturally in the Earth's crust. There are about 3000 different minerals in the Earth’s crust. Minerals
can be classified depending on their chemical makeup, crystal structure or physical properties.

Minerals can also be classified into the following four groups.

* Silicate minerals, all of which contain the elements silicon (Si) and oxygen (O), and include quartz,
feldspar, mica, garnet and tale. About 40% of the known minerals are silicates.

* Non-metallic minerals. These might contain a metal but don’t look like metals and aren’t used as
sources of metals. This group includes calcite, sulfur (S), rock salt, gypsum, fluorite and graphite (a
form of the element carbon, C) .

* Metal ore minerals are so named because they are economic sources of metals. The group includes
galena (contains lead, Pb), dolomite (contains magnesium, Mg), sphalerite (contains zinc, Zn),
bauxite (contains aluminium, Al) and haematite (contains iron, Fe).

* Gem minerals which are the precious and semi-precious stones such as opal, jade, garnet, topaz,
emerald, ruby, sapphire and diamond (the hardest naturally occurring substance),

Most rocks are made up of more than one mineral. For example, if you have two different samples of
granite, they will both contain quartz, feldspar and mica, but the proportions of each mineral will be
different. There are so many different minerals that identifying and classifying them is often difficult. Using
only one property is not of very much use because, for example, many minerals have the same shape or
colour. Several properties are, therefore, used to identify and group minerals. These properties include the
colour and the shape of crystals, cleavage (how something splits), lustre (how shiny something is), streak
test (what happens when it is rubbed on a hard surface) and hardness.

Scientific Method |

The word ‘Science’ comes from the Latin ‘scientia’, meaning ‘to know’. It is used to describe organised
knowledge. A scientist could be described as someone who studies a particular area of knowledge in a
methodical way. There are many areas of science, including astronomy, biology, chemistry, geology,
meteorology, paleontology and physics.

Scientists deal with problems in a certain way. They may notice something interesting and then try to
explain why it happens. The main way they do this is to gather more information (often by carrying out
experiments) and then make an educated guess. If this doesn’t work, they think again and perhaps try
different experiments, The following terms are often used to describe scientific method.

Observation: seeing, hearing, touching, smelling or tasting.
Inference: a judgement based on an observation.
Hypothesis: a possible explanation based on observation,
Experiment: to do something to test a hypothesis.

Results: observations/measurements from an experiment.
Conclusion: a final decision reached after doing experiments.

eee eee

Observations involve more than seeing — they can also involve hearing, smelling, touching and tasting.
Observations are quantitative when numbers are given (for example, 25°C) and qualitative when they
involve descriptions (for example, ‘hot’, ‘cold’). An hypothesis should be written as a statement which can
be proved or disproved by experiment.

Astronomy

A comet is a misty celestial object revolving around the sun in a huge elliptical orbit.
1 What is meant by a ‘celestial object’?

It has a small, solid nucleus with a long tail which points away from the sun, The most famous comet is
Halley’s Comet which came close to Earth in 1531, 1607, 1682, 1759 and so on. with its latest appearance
being in 1986,

2 When do you think Halley's Comet came near the Earth between 1758 and 1986? Explain your answer.

Nebulae are clouds of gas and dust particles. Before telescopes were used in astronomy, many star
groupings were mistakenly called nebulae because of their diffuse appearance. A famous dark nebula is
the Horsehead Nebula in Orion.

3 + ~=What is meant by ‘diffuse appearance’?

A nova (plural: novae) is literally a ‘new star’, It is actually an existing star that gets many thousands of
times brighter than normal without warning and then slowly fades back to its original brightness. A
supernova (plural: supernovae) is a star which increases its brightness billions of times and the star is
destroyed in the process. Supernovae are much rarer than novae.

4 What would happen to life on Earth if our sun became a nova?

All stars give out radiation including visible light. Astronomers analyse the light from them with a
spectroscope. This splits up light into a ‘rainbow’ spectrum of colours. Specific lines in the spectrum of an
object can tell astronomers the materials of which the object is made. An object which is moving rapidly
away from an observer has its spectrum ‘shifted’ towards the longer wavelengths, that is, red. An object
which is moving rapidly towards an observer has its spectrum ‘shifted’ towards the shorter wavelengths,
such as blue. Astronomers have discovered that the spectra from other galaxies has displayed ‘red shift’,
the further away galaxies showing the greatest ‘red shift’.

— N-3 | ASTRONOMY —
Astronomy and Australia

The view of stars and planets in the Southern hemisphere is different from the view in the Northern
hemisphere. In 1768, in command of the Endeavour, James Cook was sent to the South Pacific. He, with
a group of British astronomers, observed the transit of the planet Venus across the sun in June 1769.
Following this he charted the coasts of New Zealand, Australia and New Guinea.

The Astronomer Royal in England (Nevil Maskeleyne) expected a comet to reappear in 1789 and wanted
an observatory set up in the Southern hemisphere. He appointed Lieutenant William Dawes to travel with
the First Fleet to Australia. Dawes constructed his observatory in Sydney (at Maskeleyne Point, now known:
as Dawes Point) but the comet never appeared. His son (William Rutter Dawes) became a well-known
astronomer.

Sir Thomas Brisbane was a British soldier and astronomer who was appointed Governor of New South
Wales in 1821. His interest in astronomy began when he was nearly shipwrecked due to a navigational
error. He established an observatory in 1822 at Parramatta, near Sydney. He appointed two astronomers to
study the stars visible in the Southern hemisphere and, by 1835, they had described and classified
thousands of new stars.

Australia has had its share of famous astronomers. John Tebbutt was an amateur astronomer born in
Windsor, NSW. He started his observations in the 1850s and built his first observatory in 1863. He was the
most famous Australian astronomer of his time. He discovered two comets and was also interested in
meteorology (the atmosphere and weather).

Another notable Australian astronomer was Joseph Lade Pawsey who died in 1962. He specialised in
radioastronomy and worked for the CSIRO.

Celestial objects often give out radio waves. These are similar to light, but are of a longer wavelength and
cannot be seen. They can be detected by radio telescopes. Radio telescopes are very large, dish-shaped

The Development
of Astronomy

Astronomy: the study of planets, stars and other heavenly bodies.

Humans have always been interested in the skies, People have been frightened by comets, meteor showers,
eclipses of the sun and of the moon and so on. Many ancient civilisations came up with calendars based
‘on astronomical investigations, which they used to work out when it was time for planting, harvesting and
so on. A summary of advances in astronomy is given below.

© Almost 2000 years ago, an Egyptian astronomer named Claudius Ptolemy said the Earth was the
centre of the universe. He also stated that all objects in the sky were perfect spheres. For the next 13
centuries this idea (the Geocentric theory) was held by most people.

* A Polish monk, Nicolaus Copernicus (around 1530), came up with the idea that the sun, and not the
Earth, was the centre of our solar system. This suggestion (the Heliocentric theory) disagreed with
the beliefs of the Church at the time. His work was not published until just before his death in 1543.
It took a long time and the work of many scientists to prove that Copernicus was right.

© Tycho Brahe (1546 to 1601) was a Danish astronomer who, with the assistance of his sister Sofie,
gathered very accurate astronomical observations. He didn’t agree with all of the theories of
Copernicus. His work was used by his German assistant, Johannes Kepler (1571 to 1630), to prove
planets did not move in circular orbits, but in ellipses (ovals).

© Galileo Galilei (1564 to 1642) is credited with being the first person to
use the telescope to make astronomical observations, He saw the
Earth's moon had craters, Saturn had rings and that there were moons
orbiting Jupiter. The idea that other planets had satellites, contradicted
the idea that the Earth was the only object that had others orbiting it.

were not liked by some powerful people at the time. He was put under
confinement fro

Kangaroos

Kangaroos are furry, marsupial mammals only found in mainland
Australia and bordering islands. There are over fifty species of kangaroos.
They hop on their hind (rear) legs. Their front legs are short and the five
digits (‘fingers’) are of different sizes. Their long, powerful hind legs have
tendons that act as springs for powerful leaping. A large kangaroo can
jump over six metres in one bound and reach a top speed of nearly 50
kilometres per hour. Kangaroos can jump nearly two metres high.

Kangaroos use their long, muscular tails for balance when hopping and support when walking or sitting.
They are not normally aggressive, but can cause harm when they feel threatened, hitting out with their
forepaws and kicking with their muscular rear legs. Apart from humans and dingos, kangaroos have no
natural enemies. They were once hunted extensively for their meat and coats. Kanagaroo hunting was once
a popular sport in Australia, with hundreds of thousands killed each year. Some are still hunted in areas
where they are abundant or are a nuisance.

Kangaroos are marsupials and females have abdominal pouches. A newly born kangaroo (2.5 cm long)
makes its way slowly into the pouch. It does this by tracing a path of fur licked by the mother kangaroo.
The ‘joey’ remains in the pouch until it is six to nine months old. This pouch usually contains four
mammary glands — only two of these at a time operate to give milk. When the joey permanently leaves
the pouch, it still stays with its mother and continues to obtain milk by putting its head into her pouch,
usually for another six to nine months. Kangaroos can live for up to seven or eight years.

Kangaroos as also described as macropods, meaning they have large feet. The best known and largest
kangaroos are the giant, or great grey, kangaroo (Macropus giganteus) and the red kangaroo (Macropus
rufus). Red kangaroos tend to be found in the deserts and dry grassland of central Australia

Our Skeleton

Humans are vertebrates. This means that we have a backbone. All vertebrates have
a skeleton. A skeleton is made up of bones or cartilage (gristle) connected together
to form a semi-rigid structure. Sharks and rays have skeletons made of cartilage.
The skeleton provides support, allows movement and protects vital organs.

1 Give an example of a ‘vital organ’.

Without a skeleton we would not be able to stand upright. It allows the body to
move because many of our limbs (such as legs and arms) have joints. The main
parts of a human skeleton are the skull, ribs, vertebral column (backbone),
humerus, radius, ulna, femur, tibia, fibula, pelvis and scapula. There are 206
bones in the human skeleton.

The human skeleton has components other than bones, such as cartilage.
Cartilage is very tough — the end of the nose and the outer parts of the ears are
made of cartilage. Joints are where bones or cartilages join together. Ligaments
connect the joints of bones together. Tendons (sinews) join muscles to bones.

There are many types of joints. They include fixed joints which allow no
movement, such as in the skull. The bones of joints which move are covered in
cartilage (which is smooth) and have a lubricant called synovial fluid.

2 What does a ‘lubricant’ do?

Ball-and-socket joints (for instance the hip joint) are the most flexible joints. The movable bone can swivel
in many directions. Hinge joints (such as the knee) only allow the bone to move in one of two opposing
directions. Pivot joints only allow rotation. These are found in the elbow (between the bottom of the
humerus and the radius). Sliding (gliding) joints, are found in the wrist and ankle. In these joints the
surfaces of the bones slip a short distance over each ather.

Sometimes joints suffer ‘wear and tear’ and need to be dealt with by surgery. Silicones are useful materials
for some body-replacement parts. They resist acids, are flexible and are impervious to water.

Plant Growth and van Helmont’s
Experiment

People wondered for a long period in history how a tiny seed could grow into a large plant. They were
curious as to where all of the extra mass came from. Greek philosophers such as Aristotle (384-322 ac),
believed that plants gained their nourishment from the soil.

1 How long did Aristotle live?

It wasn’t until the seventeenth century that experiments were carried out to test the validity of this theory.
A Belgian physician, Jean-Baptiste van Helmont (1580-1644), demonstrated that soil contributes very litle
to the mass gained by plants as they grow. He placed a willow seedling of known mass into a pot which
contained a known mass of soil. He watered the plant regularly and reweighed the plant and soil after five
years, Here is a simplified version of the results of his experiment:

* mass of soil 90.9 kg
* mass of soil plus seedling 91.0 kg
* mass of soil plus plant after five years 167.6 kg
© mass of plant 76.8 kg

2 What was the mass of the willow seedling?

3 What was the change in mass of the soil?

4 Give a conclusion that could be drawn from these results.
Plants extract vital minerals from the soil, but these make up only a very small part of the mass of a plant.
Only a small amount of the water taken up by a plant is kept by the plant. Typically, over 90% of water is
lost in transpiration. This is the process by which water evaporates from plant leaves. A considerable
amount of the mass of a plant is gained from carbon dioxide absorbed from the air,

Some elements are required by plants in relatively large amounts and these are called macronutrients, The
most common of these elements are carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen. Others include sulfur,
phosphorus, calcium, potassium and magnesium. Other elements needed by plants are iron, chlorine, copper,
manganese, zinc, molybdenum, boron and nickel. These are called micronutrients or trace elements.

Properties of Water

When a substance dissolves in water to form a solution, the substance is the solute and the water is the
solvent. Water is a very important solvent — it is sometimes called the ‘universal solvent’.

1 Seawater is a solution of (mainly) sodium chloride. Name the solute and solvent in seawater.

A habitat is where an organism lives and can be aquatic or terrestrial. Aquatic habitats can be fresh or
saline (salty) and have more constant temperatures than terrestrial habitats. The smaller variations in
temperature may make aquatic habitats more favourable than land for life to survive.

Respiration

Plants and animals use sugars and oxygen in a process called
respiration to provide energy for living.

oxygen + sugars — carbon dioxide + water + energy

Respiration occurs continuously in living things, during both day and
night. For respiration to occur in cells, the sugars and oxygen must
reach the cells. Very simple animals, such as amoebas, engulf their
food by a process called phagocytosis and absorb oxygen from the
surrounding water.

More complex animals cannot simply surround their food or absorb oxygen. These animals usually have
separate systems working together to make sure that both the oxygen and the food reach the cells. Oxygen
must be obtained from the air and transported around the body, Foods need to be broken down so that the
cells can absorb the necessary nutrients.

1 Explain what is meant by ‘nutrient’.

The body's respiratory system is the system that extracts oxygen
from the air, uses the oxygen (and food) to supply energy to the cells
and returns unwanted gases to the atmosphere. These gases are
carbon dioxide, water vapour and unused oxygen,

3 Give the chemical formula for water.

You may have done some chemical tests to identify carbon dioxide, water and oxygen. Carbon dioxide
turns a solution called limewater from clear to cloudy. Water turns cobalt chloride paper from blue to pink.
Oxygen will relight a smouldering piece of wood.

In the human respiratory system, air is taken in through the nose or mouth. It travels down a long pipe
called the trachea. The trachea then splits into two bronchi which lead to the lungs. The bronchi branch
into tiny tubes called bronchioles inside each of the lungs. The bronchioles end in bubble-like air sacs
called alveoli. One alveolus is about 2 mm in diameter. Air inside each alveolus gives oxygen to the blood

Seed: the fertilised ovule of a flowering plant which is
able to germinate and produce a new plant.

Many plants begin their lives as seeds. A seed contains a store of food, an
embryo and a seed coat (testa), The embryo has the material needed to
form the shoot and root, The seed coat protects the seed. When conditions
are right, the seed grows — a process called germination — and a seedling
is formed. Water, oxygen and warmth are needed before germination can
take place.

A root comes from the embryo and grows downwards to anchor the young
plant in the soil. At the same time, a shoot grows upwards into the air.

Leaves grow on the shoot and the seedling is able to support itself.

Until this stage is reached, the seedling depends entirely on its own food
store, The stored food is used up as the seedling grows.

Seeds contain very little water and can absorb more than their own weight in water. Sometimes the seed
coat must be cracked to facilitate the absorption of water. Some seeds need to be soaked in water. Others,
such as the carob (locust bean), need to have been eaten and passed through an animal’s digestive system.
‘The seed must also have a supply of oxygen. Many seeds will fail to germinate if they are lying very deep
in the soil. This is because oxygen from the air only reaches them very slowly. All plants have a fairly
narrow range of temperatures within which they will germinate. For wheat seeds, the best temperature for
germination is between 25°C and 30°C and for maize (corn) seeds it is between 37°C and 44°C.

Some seeds are said to be dormant. The seeds are alive but waiting for the best conditions to germinate.
Dormant seeds are able to stay alive even under severe weather conditions which would kill the seedling
if germination had taken place.

Structure of Plants

When scientists talk about the structure of plants, they are usually referring to the plant's roots, stem,
leaves and flowers, Not every plant has all of these parts. We are going to look at flowering plants.

The roots anchor the plant to the earth. They help the plant extract water and minerals from the soil. Water
flows up from the roots to the leaves (where some evaporates) by a process called transpiration. The stem
helps support the plant and keep it upright. Liquids travel up and down the stem. In the stem are special
tubes called xylem which carry water and dissolved salts from the roots to the leaves in the process of
transpiration. Phloem are tubes which carry sugars (made in photosynthesis) from the leaves to other parts
of the plant. Cellulose is a complex carbohydrate and makes up the majority of the cell wall of plant cells.

The leaves are where photosynthesis takes place. There is a green pigment (colouring) in leaves called
chlorophyll, which is essential for photosynthesis. A plant is a producer organism. This means that it
manufactures its own food, During the day it respires (uses up food and generates carbon dioxide) and
photosynthesises (absorbs carbon dioxide) at the same time. During the night it just respires, Animals
cannot make food. Animals simply use food made by plants or eat other animals and, in the process, give
out carbon dioxide, Carbon dioxide (CO,) is a colourless, odourless gas which makes up less than 1% of
air. Plants help to regulate the amount of carbon dioxide in the air and, hence, affect the greenhouse effect
and the world’s climate, To enter the plant, carbon dioxide must pass through tiny holes called stomates
which are found in the largest number on the underside of leaves. They allow oxygen and carbon dioxide
to move in and out of the plant. Water vapour can also move out of the plant through stomates.

same place and need the same things to survive. It could be two species of animals eating the same food,

The Heart

The celis in your body need food, water and oxygen and must get
rid of waste products. A transport system is needed to move these
materials through the body. Your blood system does this.

The blood system consists of blood vessels (tubes) of different sizes
and a muscular heart which contracts rhythmically to pump blood
through the blood vessels. The blood system is often called the
circulatory system.

The blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart are called
arteries, Arteries have thick, muscular walls which contract in
rhythm with the heart and help force blood along. The regular
muscular contractions are your pulse, and you can feel your pulse
in your wrist and neck,

The blood vessels that carry the blood back to the heart are called veins. Veins have narrower, less muscular
walls than arteries and the pressure of the blood is lower. They are found closer to the surface of your skin,
and rely on the movement of other muscles in your body to help push blood back to the heart.

The large arteries and veins connected to the heart form numerous branches and become narrower, The
narrowest arteries and veins are connected by microscopic vessels called capillaries. Capillaries are very,
very thin (only a few cells thick) and allow substances to pass easily through their walls, This is how food,
water and dissolved oxygen pass from the blood to the cells, and how waste products from the cells pass
into the blood to be carried away,

The human heart weighs about 300 g on average, and is a pump with walls made of muscle. There are
specialised tissues in the heart that produce an electrical signal at regular intervals. This signal stimulates
rhythmic contractions of the cardiac muscle. When this muscle contracts, it squeezes blood out of the heart
and around the body. When the muscle relaxes, the heart fills with blood returning from its journey around
the body. One complete contraction and relaxation of the heart makes up a heart b

The Skin

The skin (or cutis) is the largest organ of the body. It is a protective covering and holds other organs inside
the body. The thin outer part is called the epidermis, in which cells multiply continuously and push dead
cells outward. Cells (melanocytes) in the epidermis contain a pigment (colouring matter) called melanin,
which gives the skin its colour.

In the presence of sunlight the skin produces Vitamin D, an essential ingredient for healthy bones and
teeth. Although we need to be in the sun for a certain amount of time to maintain health, too much sun
is bad for us. It can cause sunburn, dry skin and, over a period of years, cancers can develop. The major
cause of this is ultraviolet (UV) rays.

A thicker, inner layer is the dermis, or true skin, The dermis contains
connective tissue which has blood vessels, nerve endings, sweat glands,
oil glands, hair follicles, muscles and fatty tissue. The skin has many
sensations, because the nerve endings that can detect touch, heat, cold,
pressure and pain are present in it. The ends of nails and hair are dead
cells, so it does not hurt to cut them,

Oil produced in the oil (sebaceous) glands help keep the skin smooth and
soft. Hair grows from follicles (tiny tubes) that extend into the dermis
where cells divide rapidly. The length of the hair depends on the location
in the body. For example, eyelashes only grow to a certain length.

Tiny openings or pores are in the skin. These allow us to rid ourselves of waste products through
perspiration (sweat). This also helps us to maintain a steady body temperature of 37°C, When your body
is cold, muscle fibres on either side of hair follicles contract. This gives you the feeling of ‘goose bumps’.
When this happens, air is trapped between the hairs. This provides insulation and helps to keep us warm.

Water Supplies

Water is the most common liquid on Earth and controls our lives. We drink it, wash in it, fish in it and
grow crops with it. All living things need water. About two-thirds of your body is water. Every day you
need two to three litres of water. This water can be taken in as food or drink. It replaces water lost in urine,
sweat and when you breathe. People have been known to survive for more than a month without food,
but only about a week without water,

Large amounts of water are also used in industry. Most of the water is used for cooling. A large power
station uses about 5 megalitres of water per day. Because of this, power stations are often built near the
coast or near rivers to ensure a large source of water for the cooling towers. Other major uses of water are
for washing and to dissolve things. It takes about 10 litres of water to make 1 litre of beer, 200 litres to
make 1 newspaper, and 50 000 litres to make a medium-sized car. Per day, a person might use 70 litres
flushing the toilet, 50 litres for personal washing, 25 litres for clothes washing, 15 litres for dishwashing,
12 litres for gardening and carwashing, 5 litres for cooking and 3 litres for drinking.

Before water reaches us, it has been purified by the water authorities but, originally, it will come from
either surface water (rivers and lakes) or ground water in underground wells. If we trace the water supply
back even further, then the source of all this water is rain.

Sewage is the main cause of water pollution. If the amount of sewage is small, then bacteria in the water
can break it down into less harmful materials such as carbon dioxide, nitrates and water. If the amount of
sewage is too large, then the bacteria use up all of the oxygen dissolved in it as they feed on the sewage.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY 12

Using amino acid sequences to
define evolutionary relationships

Introduction
Classification in biology is largely based on the structural characteristics of organisms. Organisms with similar
structures are placed in the same group as it is assumed that they are closely related to each other and share a
relatively recent common ancestor. However, it is often unclear which structural characteristics are more
important from an evolutionary point of view. Also, comparing structural characteristics is not generally helpful
when species are very different. The study of the biochemical similarities between organisms has recently
become possible and has provided new evidence about evolutionary relationships.

Biochemical studies have made it possible to compare the biochemicals (such as proteins and nucleic acids) in
various species. The degree of difference between the same protein or nucleic acid in different species provides
‘a measure of the length of time since the two species shared a common ancestor. This is because mutations occur
relatively regularly. So, the longer it is since a common ancestor, the greater the difference between molecules.
It is this information that can be used in conjunction with fossils and other evidence to piece together
evolutionary relationships.

component of the biochemical pathway of aerobic respiration and is present in all modern organisms except
anaerobic bacteria. Cytochrome C molecules each contain approximately 100 amino acids and the exact
sequence of those amino acids is known for about 60 species.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY

The adaptations of mangroves

Introduction

Mangroves are trees that form woody plant communities in shallow tidal water. They live on sheltered shores in
bays, estuaries and the sheltered side of offshore islands. They make an essential contribution to the ecology of
coastal and marine environments. Their roots provide habitats for many marine animals such as crabs, prawns,
bamacles, isopods and amphipods, as well as helping to trap nutrient-rich silts and preventing erosion of the bank.
‘Their canopy provides a habitat for about 35 species of insect and many birds that eat mangrove nectar and pollen.
Mangroves are specifically adapted to their tidal environment. This environment includes soil (mud) that is
always waterlogged with salty water and a varying water level caused by tides ebbing and flowing underneath
the mangroves. These conditions would kill other land plants. So how do mangroves survive?

Aim
To describe the adaptations of mangroves to their tidal environment and explain how these adaptations help
Mangroves to survive.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY 13

The mutagenic nature
of Agent Orange

Introduction
Mutagens are substances that can cause permanent mutations. Mutations are changes to DNA: the genetic
material responsible for controlling reproduction and the development of life. Once a mutation has occurred in
a strand of DNA, the mutation will be replicated every time the cell divides. Mutations may be beneficial, harmful
‘or may have no obvious effect. One of the harmful effects of mutations is the formation of some cancer cells.
Mutations do occur naturally, but mutagenic substances make them occur more frequently.

During the Vietnam War in the late 1960s, the US military sprayed an estimated 95 milion litres of Agent Orange (a
herbicide mix) on about 10 percent of the area of southern Vietnam. Agent Orange has since been found to contain
significant amounts of the chemical dioxin: a known mutagen. Many Vietnam War veterans have subsequently
suffered from a range of medical problems that have been attributed to their exposure to Agent Orange.

Aim
To investigate the mutagenic nature of Agent Orange.

Date
Agent Orange is the code name for a herbicide developed for the United States military which was primarily used in tropical

climates. Although the genesis of the product goes back to the 1940s, serious testing for military applications did not begin
until the early 1960s. Agent Orange is a 50:50 mix of two chemicals:

 2,4-dichlorophenoxy acetic acid (2,4-D) and
 2,45-trichtorophenoxy acetic acid (2,4,5-T)
The combined product was mixed with kerosene or diesel fuel and sprayed from aircraft, vehicles and by hand,

Agent Orange was effective in defoliating (killing the leaves) and ultimately killing broad-teaf trees and shrubs in the dense
jungles in Southeast Asia. The goal of the largest military defoliation campaign in history was to deny the enemy food or cover
in dense forests.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY

Using pedigrees to determine
the inheritance of genetic diseases

Introduction

Genetic diseases occur in most human populations and arise due to mutations that create a deleterious (harmful)
gene in one individual. If the deleterious gene is dominant, it will die out if it prevents people from reaching a
breeding age. However, if it is recessive, it may remain in a population and get carried by heterozygous people
and only appear in a homozygous individual.

Pedigrees can be used to determine whether diseases that seem to run in families are genetically inherited. By
looking at a pedigree of a famity with a history of a genetic disease, you can identify patterns of inheritance from
which you can determine whether it is dominant or recessive. You can also use pedigrees to predict the likelihood
that the children of two individuals will have the genetic disease. This information can be used in genetic
counselling where partners can determine the risk of a genetically inherited disease appearing in their offspring.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY 17

The quality of drinking water

Introduction

Providing water to any population of people is critical. It is even more critical when a big city is involved. In
Sydney, for example, Sydney Water provides approximately 1500 million litres of water each day to more than
3.7 million people. An integrated network of 15 dams and storage reservoirs with associated catchments, eight
water filters, more than 20,000 kilometres of water mains and canals, 162 pumping stations and 262 service
reservoirs are used to gather, store and transport water. In addition to supplying a large quantity of water, they
must also supply a high quality of water.

Aim
To understand how drinking water is monitored and treated to ensure that it is safe for human consumption.

Raw water

Raw water is groundwater and water in rivers, streams and lakes that has not been treated to ensure that it is suitable for
human consumption. Such walers can contain contaminants such as sediment, salts, organic material and pathogens such
as Giardia. The level of treatment required to make the water suitable for human consumption depends on the overall
Condition of the catchment area (the area of land that catches the water and over which it flows to reach the storage place),

undisturbed by people and livestock. Water from these areas requires less treatment than those from catchments that
have been used for other purposes such as agriculture, urban development or forestry. Waters from these disturbed
Catchments can be severely degraded and thus require more intensive levels of treatment. In addition, raw water from
some sources may require pre-treatment to remove other contaminants.

Temperature control and
water loss in humans

Introduction

Humans, like birds and other mammals, are endothermic. The human body is maintained at a relatively constant

temperature by a number of mechanisms:

+ Ifthe core temperature drops, the body can limit heat loss by constricting (narrowing) the peripheral blood
vessels (in the skin), raising body hair and generating extra heat by shivering.

* If the core temperature rises, the body can lose heat by sweating. As the sweat evaporates, it cools the skin
and the blood flowing through the skin. This process is made more efficient by dilating (widening) the
peripheral blood vessels so that more blood comes in contact with the cooled skin layer.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY

Temperature regulation in
ectotherms and endotherms

Introduetion

The body temperature of ectothermic (‘warmed from the outside’) animals is determined by the temperature of
their environment. Ectotherms are unable to maintain the same level of activity when the environmental
temperature changes. In extreme cold, for example, ectotherms become too cold to move and, as the
‘environment warms their bodies, they become more active. In contrast, endothermic (‘warmed from the inside’)
‘organisms generally maintain a constant body temperature despite changes in environmental temperature.
Being endothermic enables animals to maintain activity in a wide range of environmental temperatures.

‘Animals that live in deserts experience extreme daily variations in temperature—from below zero in the early
morning up to more than 40°C in the afternoon. Animals that live high in alpine areas experience months of
extremely low temperatures followed by months of more moderate temperatures. Even in summer, temperatures
often drop below freezing at nights.

Animals usually have several adaptations to survive in the range of temperatures they experience in their habitats.
These adaptations may by structural (features of the structure of the body), behavioural (specific behaviours) or
physiological (features of the inner workings of the body). The adaptations for the regulation of body
temperature in endotherms differ greatly to those in ectotherms. In order to maintain a constant body
temperature, endothermic animals have a number of adaptations to help them retain heat when it is cold or lose
heat when it is hot. Ectotherms often have adaptations that help them to maximise the beneficial and minimise
the adverse effects of changes in environmental temperatures.

Aim
To use secondary data to identify adaptations that help regulate the body temperature of ectothermic and
endothermic animals from desert and alpine environments.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY

The effects of temperature
and pH on enzyme activity

Introduction

Enzymes are proteins that act as catalysts for the thousands of chemical reactions that occur in living things.
‘Without enzymes, these chemical reactions would not happen in the coordinated way needed to sustain life.
“There are a large number of enzymes in every cell of every living thing, and each enzyme works on a specific
chernical reaction.

Each enzyme has an optimum range of conditions (which include temperature and pH) at which its activity is
greatest. The activity of the enzyme will be much less outside the optimum range. The optimum range depends
‘on the type of organism and the part of the organism in which the enzyme is found.

In animals, a number of enzymes are involved in digestion, Two examples are:

‘* Rennin—an enzyme present in the stomachs of young mammals that causes milk solids (called curds) to
separate from the liquid in milk (called whey). This separation into curds and whey is the first step in the
digestion of milk. Junket tablets contain rennin,

‘© Pepsin is an enzyme in the stomach of many mammals that begins the breakdown of protein.

Aim

IEE To compare the effect of temperature on the enzymes of endothermic and ectothermic animals.
HEZBE To investigate the effect of temperature on the activity of the digestive enzyme rennin.

The smallpox story

Introduction

"Smallpox was always present, filing the churchyard with corpses, tormenting with constant fear all whom it had not yet
stricken, leaving on those whose lives it spared the hideous traces of its power, turning the babe into a changeling at which
the mother shuddered, and making the eyes and cheeks of the betrothed maiden objects of horror to the lover.”

Macaulay 1800

‘Smallpox is a viral disease spread by droplet infection that has killed millions of people in epidemics that started
thousands of years before Christ. The world’s first vaccine was developed for smallpox and the disease is now
almost totally eradicated,

Variolation Is an early form of vaccination. It involves taking some fluid from a person suffering from a mild bout
of smallpox and rubbing it into scratches on a healthy person, Following variolation, a smallpox rash usually
appeared and, in some cases, became a serious bout of smallpox. However, it was widely believed that variolation

gave some immunity to smallpox.

Aim
To explore the history of smallpox on Earth.

430 BC— Thucydides observed in Athens that those once infected with smallpox became immune.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY

Water balance in
terrestrial environments

Introduction

Water balance occurs when the amount of water gained by the animal is balanced by the amount of water they
lose over a given period of time. Terrestrial animals gain water from their diet (including food and drink) and
from the oxidation of carbohydrates, fats and proteins in their cells (such as by cellular respiration). They lose
water when it evaporates from their skin and respiratory system and in their faeces and urine.

The amount of available water in terrestrial environments varies greatly. In arid environments such as deserts, where
the amount of available water is usually extremely small, animals have a range of adaptations to maintain water
balance. Kangaroo rats generally live in arid environments whereas laboratory rats live in a controlled environment.

Aim

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY

Adaptation of the Wompoo Fruit
Dove to environmental conditions

Introduction

The Wompoo Fruit Dove (Ptilinopus magnificus) is a species of bird that lives in the rainforests of eastern Australia
and New Guinea. Scientists have named several subspecies (the name of a subspecies is the third word in its
scientific name) of Wompoo Fruit Dove from different locations. These subspecies vary only slightly from one
another in their markings but vary markedly in size. All subspecies of the Wompoo Fruit Dove are endangered,
largely due to the destruction of their rainforest habitat.

Rainforests exist only in warm places where rainfall and humidity are high all year round. Rainforests are very
diverse places that support a large number of species in their moist, humid environment. Wompoo Fruit Doves
eat the abundant fruit in the rainforest and rarely move more than a few kilometres away from their place of
birth in their lifetime.

Aim

To identify the trend in the size of Wompoo Fruit Doves from different locations and explain how this trend may
have evolved.

Hypothesis

An investigation into the effect of pH on seedling growth experiment

Purpose To investigate the effect of pH on seedling growth.

Procedure

Germinate 20 seed pods on damp cotton wool.
Choose 12 seedlings with a height of about 12 mm.

Plant each seedling in a pot of the same size. For each pot, use 80 g of
quality potting mix and water with 12 mL of tap water.

Label each pot with the pH treatment the soil will receive: 4 pots with
pH 5, 4 pots with pH 7 and 4 pots with pH 9.

Weigh each pot to the nearest 0.1 g. Draw up a data table and record the
results for each pot in the column for day 0.

Keep plants in the same position where light is available to maintain
lighting conditions.

Reweigh the seedlings in their pots 2 days later. Record the results for
each pot in the column for day 2.

Immediately after each weighing, give each plant 10mL of water at the
appropriate pH according to the label on the pot.
Repeat steps 5 and 6 every 2 days for the next 10 days

1 INTRODUCTION TO FORENSIC SCIENCE

Even the best experts in the world cannot solve a crime without evidence. Therefore, it is essential
that the scene of the crime be treated in the correct way.

A. Securing the crime scene

In most cases the first police officer on the
scene will be a uniformed police officer. They
are not usually trained as detectives and so
should touch as little as possible of the crime
scene and the area in the vicinity. All
precautions should be taken to avoid any
accidental destruction or contamination of
potential evidence.

The officer who arrives on the scene first will
ensure the safety of any injured people and of
the site itself. This may involve turning off gas,
water and electricity supplies. Ideally, the site
should be secured with a physical barrier, so
that no unauthorised people can enter. This will
leave the site as close as possible to the state it
was in at the time of the crime, preserving all
traces left by the criminals for the officers
tained in searching for evidence.

Where it is obvious that a person is dead, the body is not touched or moved in any way until it has
been carefully examined and photographed. Where there are injured people involved, the police officer
will see to their safety and call an ambulance before asking for the appropriate police backup. While
waiting, the uniformed officer may record the names and addresses of any eyewitnesses to the crime.

B. Examining the scene

If a major crime has been committed, then the next person on the scene will probably be the senior
detective in charge of the investigation. A police surgeon and/or a pathologist may be called in if
a body is involved. Specially trained crime scene investigators (CSIs), also called scene of crime
officers (SOCOs), who are experts at looking for evidence, are called in at an early stage of the
investigation.

photography, will take pictures (still and

and spectroscopy
2 CONTACT TRACES

A simple small instrument called a spectroscope can be used by scientists to produce a very clear
spectrum. It was first developed in the 1850s by German scientists Robert Kirchoff and Robert
Bunsen. It consists of a long brass tube with a prism at one end.

These scientists found that if some elements were heated, they began to glow and produce light of
their own characteristic colour. If they allowed the light to pass through the spectroscope, the light
separated into a series of distinct bright lines of various colours.

The normal visible spectrum is a continuous spectrum, where one colour merges into the next. It
can be seen if the spectroscope is held up to normal light. The spectrum produced by heating
different chemicals is called a line spectrum, because it is a series of bright coloured lines, separated

2 - 2 Fibres and fabrics

2 CONTACT TRACES

If loose fibres found at the crime scene have not come from the victim, they may have come from a
large number of sources—from the perpetrator's clothes, from carpet or curtains where the crime
occurred, or even from a rug or blanket in which the body was wrapped for transportation, if the body
was moved. Also, fibres from the victim may have been deposited on the perpetrator, and these will be
looked for on all suspects. Any such fibres found could connect the suspect with the crime scene.

Fibres can be either synthetic (man-made)—such as nylon, rayon, terylene, polyester—or they can be
natural, being made from either plants (cotton and linen) or from animals (wool, silk and mohair).
Generally, under the microscope, natural fibres have a rougher surface, taper from root to tip and appear

somewhat irregular. Cotton fibres are actually collapsed tubes, while wool fibres, like hair, have scales.
On the other hand, synthetic fibres are smooth and even and have a much longer length (staple).

also vary. Often, both the strength and thickness of any fibres found at a crime scene are measured
in the forensic laboratory and compared with any found on a suspect. The melting point of a
synthetic fibre is usually measured and its colour analysed. If two fibres look the same under the
microscope, have the same thickness, strength, colour and melting point, then they probably both
came from the same source. If the fibres are uncommon, then two matching fibres are even more
likely to have come from the same garment,

| = 6 The forensic

science laboratory
1 INTRODUCTION TO FORENSIC SCIENCE X

The forensic scientist, employed full-time by the police department, is the analyst back in the
laboratory. They usually do not attend the crime scene. Their main responsibility is to help the police
investigation by using their specialist knowledge and techniques. Forensic scientists usually have a
science degree from a university, with specialist training and experience on top of that. They are often
not police officers and they do not usually interview witnesses or suspects; interviewing is left to the
police officers.

Many forensic scientists specialise in a certain
area such as fingerprint identification, DNA
profiling or forgery detection. It is the forensic
scientist who can identify whether a hair is
human or animal and can identify from what
part of the body it came. A forensic scientist
who specialises in ballistics can often identify
the exact gun from which a bullet was fired.

The forensic laboratory houses many pieces of
expensive and specialised equipment to help
the scientist analyse the evidence.

Once an item arrives at the laboratory, the
forensic scientist decides what tests or analysis
it should undergo, and in what order. Some tests
will destroy part or all of the evidence, while
other tests will not affect the sample at all.
Obviously, all non-destructive tests should be
carried out first. The scientist needs to know the
information required by the investigating
officers in order to select the appropriate tests.

‘To prevent cross-contamination in the laboratory, all evidence from the crime scene is stored in a
different place to any items taken from a suspect's home or car. Items from the different scenes are
analysed by different forensic scientists where possible, and always on different days and in
different rooms.

2-10 Glass Q

2 CONTACT TRACES

Glass is a material that is made mostly from sand. For practical uses it is usually clear and
transparent. It can be made to be heat resistant, coloured, stronger, more brittle or more flexible by
just changing the amounts of the other chemicals that are added to the silica from the sand. The
mixture is heated to a very high temperature so that all the substances melt together. When forensic
scientists are asked to compare fragments of glass from a crime scene, there are a number of tests
which they may carry out. These include inspection under UV light, and a measurement of its
density and refractive index.

Some glass samples will fluoresce under UV light, so this test would be carried out first. Density is
a measure of how closely the particles of a material are packed together. If a type of glass contains
a lot of lead then it would tend to be denser than one with very little lead. The density of a sample
can be compared by finding in what liquids a sample will float. If the glass is placed in a liquid like
water or methylated spirits and sinks, we know it is denser than these liquids. If it floats on top of
a dense liquid like glycerine, then we know it is less dense than glycerine. If the glass neither sinks
nor floats in a certain liquid, or mixture of liquids, then its density must be exactly the same as the
liquid, Now, if two glass fragments were both suspended in the same liquid, then they would have
exactly the same density, and may have come from the same source. Comparison of densities is not
used as often in the forensic laboratory as in previous years, because glass manufacture today is more
automated and density characteristics do not vary as much as they did years ago when each factory
had its own ‘recipe’.

I. 7 Going to trial

1_INTRODUCTION TO FORENSIC SCIENCE

In court the suspect, the person police believe carried out
the crime, is put on trial before a jury for major crimes, and
before a magistrate for less serious crimes. It is often the
quality of the police evidence that will influence the
opinion of both the jury and the magistrate.

In a jury trial, the judge is there to listen and pass sentence
if the jury decides that the accused is guilty. The
prosecution lawyer puts forward the police case and calls
any expert witnesses to give their opinion in order to
convince the jury of the facts of the case.

The defence lawyer must try to defend the person charged
with the crime by trying to point out any holes in the
prosecution's argument and to try to put doubt in the jury
members’ minds. Only the jury can decide if the accused is
guilty or not, beyond any reasonable doubt. An expert witness may also be called in by the defence
to discredit the case against a suspect.

The scientific evidence must be presented in a way that can be understood by the court, and not in
a way that may confuse it. Judges, lawyers and juries do not usually have a deep knowledge of
science, so all scientific results have to be presented in non-technical terms. This is why photographs,
videos, maps and plaster casts are so important.

Because of the court’s lack of scientific expertise, the forensic scientist or expert witness must be
prepared to give an expert opinion on what the evidence implies—that is, they must be able to say how
likely it is that the crime is linked to the suspect who has been charged. They may give an opinion of
the probability of the soil found on the suspect's shoe coming from the crime scene, or the suspect's
fingerprint matching one found on some stolen property, hence linking the suspect to the crime.

The forensic scientist not only needs to be qualified and experienced in their field of expertise, they
also need to be accepted by the court as having a relia

2-4 Hair

Although hair cannot usually identify a single individual as fingerprints can, hair found at a crime
scene can be very useful. Besides giving some indication of age, race and sex, hairs found at a crime
scene can strengthen the links between a suspect and that scene.

Human hair can be classified into six groups, according to its origin:

Hair from the scalp tends to have a circular cross-section, often with somewhat split ends.
Beard hair often has a more triangular cross-section.

Eyebrows and eyelashes also have a circular cross-section, but their ends are tapered.
Under-arm hair has a more oval cross-section than the other types.

Pubic hair is often short, curly and stiff, with an oval or triangular cross-section and short roots.
General body hair is finer and softer than pubic hair, but is also curly and either triangular or
oval in cross-section.

Hair is composed mainly of the protein keratin, which is very difficult to destroy except by fire and
certain chemicals. It will remain preserved in the grave longer than most of the body except for the
bones. Microscopic inspection of hair can also indicate whether hair was pulled out, cut off or
whether it just fell out naturally.

forensic laboratory
1_ INTRODUCTION TO FORENSIC SCIENCE

Still one of the most commonly used and most important tools in the forensic laboratory is the

microscope, The simplest microscope is a magnifying lens which has been used for over 100 years
to examine anything from fingerprints to footprints. It can magnify objects x 10 to x 20.

The common compound microscope found in
all schools is another useful but relatively
inexpensive piece of equipment used regularly in
the forensic laboratory. It is used when a
magnification of up to x 1000 is needed. It has
two lenses, an eyepiece lens at the top through
which the scientist looks, and an objective lens
at the lower end of the barrel, near the object
being examined. Most compound microscopes
have three or four objective lenses of different Fig. 1. Magnifying lens
powers of magnification that can be selected by
rotating them. Hairs, fibres, glass fragments,
pollen grains and fingerprint samples are all
commonly examined under such a microscope.

If even greater magnification is required, then
an electron microscope may be used. Relying
on a beam of electrons rather than visible light,
this instrument can give images of molecules
and even atoms, It can magnify up to x 200 000
and can be used to examine soil bacteria or
pollen grains to show up the smallest
difference. Generally these instruments are not
found in a forensic laboratory so scientists must
send material away to be examined under an

electron microscope if they believe that this will
reveal important information. Fig. 2 A compound microscope
